en: Had worked to make it proof against shots.
Orenburg and Margilan—
She had the lands between them searched.
The fine cloth from that region,
That formidable, bold woman
Had brought by force.
She had fine sand sifted,
Against my father Temir Khan,
Had it laid in many layers.
Such was the clothing for war:
She had thin iron wire worked into it,
Making shots from the short gun powerless.
Worn in a shooting battle, no shot pierced it;
Worn in a joust, no spear pierced it;
In sword fighting, no blade cut it.
Such was the precious garment.
He clothed them in battle dress.
When they put those clothes on,
What had been exposed was covered;
Their dignity was thus restored.
Raising their hands, crying aloud,
They pleaded with your orphan.
To keep lice from infesting them,
Separate changes against lice,
He had them put on underneath.
Ceremonial clothes were set apart;
He clothed them in ceremonial dress.
Your dear son of Manas,
Revealing his prowess then,
Transformed them with the coats he gave!
In the foothills, blaze-headed horses,
Thoroughbreds and coursers together,
Fine beasts left by his father Manas—
The forty guards and Bölökbai,
He mounted them on their choice of these.
(Truly created by God—
Have you seen that he is His servant,
Of poor Sultan Manas,
Have you seen that he is the son?)
From joy, the forty guards
Were running about there.
There their leopard father Manas
Stood alive again.
Meanwhile, a wondrous thing:
My dear mother Kanykei
Had left another store of goods.
‘Should my orphan
Grow to full strength and become a warrior,
Equal to the sons of warriors,
And come to dwell in Talas,
Should a weighty dispute arise,
Should a troublesome enemy confront him,
He might fall needlessly into suffering.
When that future day comes,
He will see these and take them as gifts.’
There was much equipment for war,
Left by my dear mother Kanykei.
Then the lacquered spears she had hidden—
Forty spears for forty guards,
Semetey took and gave.
Forty swords for these forty men
Semetey gave as well.
Forty guns for forty guards
Semetey also gave.
If you looked at the forty guards,
Their bearing, their appearance,
Their look mounted upon horses,
Drew the eyes of all who saw.
As though their sovereign, dear lion Manas,
Were still present, they appeared.
What the forty guards wore—
No shot could pierce it in a clash.
What the forty guards rode—
No shot could catch them in a crisis.
Their banners fluttered;
Black-bladed battle-axes
Flashed at their wrists.
The forty guards' winged steeds
Were all alike in their dun color,
With amulet-shaped marks upon their brows.
If you looked at the forty guards,
All were equally outstanding,
Their appearance unlike other men.
Then Semetey,
The boy, spoke these words:
“My bringer of good fortune, Bölökbai,
My support left by my father,
Let us put the day in writing;
Let us set the appointed time.
To my kinsmen Abyke and Köbösh,
I am going to see them.
If those dogs rant too much,
I am going to meet death at their hands.
My father's countless possessions,
I am going to take them.
I have reached twelve years of age,
I, the orphan left by my khan father Manas.
To my elder kinsmen's homes,
I am going to go.
If there are good, reasonable words,
I am going to agree.
If there is honesty in them,
This dear, fierce mother of mine,
To one of my six elder kinsmen,
I am going to give her.
My father Manas's remaining kin,
Elders, I am going to see them.
If I turn back safely,
If I return without dying or disappearing,
I shall stay there thirty days.
I shall travel back for ten days;
I shall stay in Bukhara for ten days;
I shall journey for ten days.
From beginning to end, that much—
I shall come in sixty days.
If I am gone beyond sixty days,
I shall have met my death.
If I am kept safe from death,
I shall return and see you.
Khan Bölökbai, forty guards,
If I am gone beyond eighty days,
Shoot wild sheep and eat them.
My support left by Manas,
Say that I have died.
If I come in sixty days,
God has granted your wish.
If I am gone beyond sixty days,
My allotted death has come; I have died.”
Giving coats that were not torn,
Giving peerless winged steeds,
Making the promise promptly,
Setting this many days as the time,
“Keep my only one safe;
If my mirror, my orphan, returns,
If God grants my wish,”
Praying thus and sobbing,
All forty guards
Cried aloud in supplication.
To Jar-Kiya of Jangirik,
By a path for beasts in single file,
They took the road toward the river.
All forty guards
Played with the horn striker, raising dust;
All made a great commotion.
To shoot roe deer if bored,
And if not bored, the forty guards
Would stay and keep their watch.
Their wretched hearts were gladdened;
They had at last seen safe and well
The boy left by Manas.
Crying, ‘Oh God!’ they swore,
Made their promise firm,
And went to the appointed place.
Kayipchi's dark ridge,
They firmly held it now.
They camped at their ease,
As though your bloodthirsty, fierce Manas
Had come alive again.
They patrolled and scouted the road,
And whole otter pelts
They put upon their trouser cuffs.
Eating yearlings suckled by barren mares,
Eating rich fat from wethers,
The lame smith and forty guards,
Until the lord's son returned,
Kayipchi's dark ridge—
There they chose to stand guard.
Their brows thus cleared;
There they became as sultans.
Let us leave them thus,
And of leopard Bakai and Semetey,
Let us begin the tale from here.
He taught what was unknown,
That learned elder Bakai.
He made the unperceived understood,
Falcon Bakai, the saint.
His knowledge was proven among the people,
My falcon, the support left by Manas.
His deeds were bright, his worth proven,
Support of the ancient sovereign,
A guiding star from the sky,
For Manas, gone to the other world,
He would think and find the counsel—
Renowned Bakai, his companion.
That fierce Bakai of yours
Drew the gaze when seen.
As one looked, Khan Bakai
Appeared like Opol Mountain.
Placed at the front, he brought good fortune;
My elder Bakai was like countless hosts.
Once he put on battle dress,
His supporter was Khojosan,
His guides, the forty hidden saints.
He appeared in his true form.
“My elder's protectors
Are equal to my father Manas's,” he thought.
Thus the boy's attention was drawn.
Good heavens, Kökcholok beneath him—
The wind could not match his trot.
That day, Kökcholok,
No beast could match his walk.
When he came to stony ground,
Stones crumbled like charcoal.
Here and there, clods from his hooves
Whistled above his head.
When he came to a hollow,
The heads of fescue rattled.
Seeing this, Semetey,
The warrior, stood grieving.
“This is God's decree.
This horse of my elder
Was a winged steed from the first.
What must he have been in his youth?
Herding camels amid shouts,
His back grew sore, his color faded.
Losing his mane and tail,
This year he was named Kökcholok.
Has the fine beast fallen into disgrace?”
Grieving at the sight of Kökcholok,
The orphan stood thus now.
Accomplished Khan Bakai
Now began to speak:
“Abyke and Köbösh, my kinsmen,
I knew their every deed.
Your father, gone to the other world,
My friend for the hereafter—
I have honored his spirit.
Their harshness I knew long ago;
The fierce one gone to the other world,
I have honored his spirit.
‘When he reaches twelve,
Will my orphan come?’ I wondered,
My heart burning for you.
I speak at length, orphan; listen.
I still have more to tell.
When Abyke and Köbösh opened my treasury,
Kanykei, on whom I relied,
Fled wandering to Bukhara.
When the Almighty brought it upon us,
Damn it, such is the world!
When your Bakai was left herding camels,
To seize the camels as booty,
Your old elder Bakai
To capture, then live at ease,
To perform this exploit,
To kill me thus,
Those dogs together drew their bows,
When they came together and besieged me,
We exchanged shots without sparing our lives,
And suffered hardship.
Without rest by day or night,
We fought without a pause.
They came within reach; I shot.
I shot all sixty of them.
I still have more to tell:
On the coming Day of Judgment,
